newsitem.title: USA: Truce seen possible in soft-drink price war.
newsitem.headline: Truce seen possible in soft-drink price war.

text.p: Peace may be about to break out in a four-month price war among major soft-drink makers.
"They're trying to declare a truce," Roy Burry, an Oppenheimer & Co. analyst, said on Thursday.
Soft-drink prices have declined for about four months, but analysts welcomed a report in a trade publication that Coca-Cola Enterprises Inc. plans a price increase after the Fourth of July holiday.
The report appeared in this week's Beverage Digest, which said in a news release Wednesday that it based its story on an internal memo obtained from Coca-Cola Co.'s biggest bottler.

As quoted in Beverage Digest, the memo said that after the July 4 holiday, "we will again attempt to raise prices.... If the competition views this as an opportunity to gain (market) share through predatory pricing, we will, as we have in the past, respond immediately."

According to industry data, a two-liter bottle of Pepsi Cola cost 99 cents in supermarkets on April 20, down from $1.03 a year earlier. A similar bottle of Coca-Cola also sold for 99 cents, down from $1.01 a year earlier.
Analysts saw the signal that prices may start to firm as good news for the bottom lines of Coca-Cola and rival PepsiCo Inc. .
"Everybody's interested in making a reasonable profit," said Prudential Securites analyst George Thompson. "Across the board, I think you'll see the pricing strengthen."
Coca-Cola Co, which owns 44 percent of Coca-Cola Enterprises, referred questions about the memo and pricing strategy to the bottler, which did not immediately return telephone calls.

The memo, which denied that Coke was responsible for the price war, was dated June 5, the day after PepsiCo executives complained to analysts about "irrational" pricing by Coca-Cola. PepsiCo shares fell more than two points that day on the news.

But on Thursday, shares of the soft-drink companies reached new highs for the year. At midday, PepsiCo shares were at $38.75, up $1. Coca-Cola Co. was up $1.375 at $79.875 Coca-Cola Enterprises was up 75 cents at $22.25, all on the New York Stock Exchange.
Cadbury Schweppes Plc, which owns the Dr Pepper and Seven Up soft-drink brands, was up 7-1/2 pence at 533-1/2 on the London Stock Exchange.

Burry said the price war started when Coca-Cola tried to gain market share by lowering prices while PepsiCo was preoccupied with other matters, such as deciding to spin off its restaurants into a separate company.
"Things got out of hand and we ended up with a big price war," Burry said.
